I have been a user of neo-office (an earlier open office fork for Mac) for years. I love it. I haven't bothered with ms office for over a decade. I checked out libre office a long time ago and it felt clunky compared to neo-office. I am really liking this release though.

As for the review... I don't get the writer's emphasis on UI. I switched away from MS before the ribbon and still can't believe it is the dominant platform. I fired up this version of libre office and knew right where to find everything to get to work.

MS Office is the dominant platform despite the ribbon because MS Office was the dominant platform before it. I barely use Office at my job(mostly basic Outlook) and even then the ribbon bullshit shows its clunkiness(why oh why do I have to open up the compose email box to edit my signatures?). Frankly, I'm pretty sure they only made the change because Open Office was getting too popular and getting everybody used to a warped UI would make switching even harder.

But I suppose he's also on about UI because the heavy reliance on menus is out of step with the way many modern applications are going: after Chrome came out, it seems like "menu" became a four letter word and everybody rushed to get rid of theirs at the expense of usability("but look at how clean our interface is!"). There aren't words strong enough in the English language to describe that trend.

MS Office was a default set of application in our system images at work, but frankly most functions were overkill for our average users. We also had a shitty email system so we decided to switch to Google Apps for Business.

Now, MS Office isn't preinstalled and most users at work are using Google Drive for basic word processing, spreadsheets, etc. If someone needs MS Office, they have to justify it and their department will assume the licensing cost. But we also offer LibreOffice in case it might suit their needs.

It almost certainly is overkill - which is probably why Microsoft moved to try and add UI to their lock in, since many of the necessary functions are interspersed with the unused ones in all suites and keeping the same interface would've made switching easy(witness Sun's buying StarOffice since it was cheaper than licensing MS Office). When you offer the reduced functionality that's actually used, on the other hand, that mostly goes away(not that I see my workplace adopting Google anything - we're a bit big for that and a bit hyperparanoid beside).
Don't worry, we are a bit paranoid in some sectors and we use GPG for sensitive documents/emails.
